{"id": "39:55/q13", "question": "What reports explain the revelation of this passage?", "turns_on": "The reports differ about those concerned and whether the Wahshi report covers three verses or verses 53–59.", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q13/p1", "position": "After the Prophet reached Medina, verses 39:53–55 were revealed about persecuted Muslims who had apostatized and despaired of repentance.", "reasons": "Umar says they and others believed God would accept neither repentance nor expiation. In Ibn Hisham and Ibn Kathir, Umar copied the revealed passage and sent it to Hisham ibn al-As; Hisham repeatedly read it at Dhu Tuwa, prayed for understanding, recognized it concerned his group's self-talk, and went to join the Prophet in Medina."}, {"id": "39:55/q13/p2", "position": "Three verses beginning with 'My servants who transgressed' were revealed in Medina about Wahshi and his companions.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq transmits this from Ata ibn Yasar in al-Tabari; al-Durr also reports Ata. Study Quran says many commentators connect verses 53–55 with Wahshi, who gained freedom by killing Hamzah at Uhud."}, {"id": "39:55/q13/p3", "position": "Verses 39:53–59 were all revealed concerning Wahshi.", "reasons": "Study Quran attributes this wider span to other commentators."}]}
{"id": "39:55/q14", "question": "How does this verse fit the surrounding call to repentance?", "turns_on": "The notes trace both the immediate link to repentance in 39:53–54 and the later consequences of accepting or rejecting that call.", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q14/p1", "position": "It elaborates the preceding call to turn to God, joining hope and the ban on despair to prompt repentance, submission and action.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reads the conjunction and imperative as pressing prompt action after 39:53; Islahi says verse 55 develops 39:54. Al-Tabataba'i calls the seven verses one discourse: the ban on despair prepares the later commands, so the first verse is no isolated promise. He describes the whole passage as calling to Islam and revelation, warning against arrogance and regret, and showing mercy. Islahi urges turning to the forgiving God rather than despair or seek deities and intercessors."}, {"id": "39:55/q14/p2", "position": "The command and warning prepare the later contrast between believers' salvation and disbelievers' loss and regret.", "reasons": "Study Quran connects verses 54–67 to the final contrast in the hereafter. Islahi says idolaters' reliance on polytheism and intercession hastens ruin; they must turn sincerely and follow the Book before later regret and wishes to believe become useless. Al-Tabataba'i likewise notes the contrast and warning against excess and arrogance."}]}
{"id": "39:55/q15", "question": "What practical urgency does the warning teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q15/p1", "position": "Submit, repent and put revelation into practice before punishment removes the chance and regret becomes useless.", "reasons": "Muqatil and al-Tabari urge obedience before surprise; Ibn Kathir and Elmalili urge following the Qur'an now. Al-Baydawi stresses remaining time to recover, while al-Biqa'i says anticipated regrets would help one avoid their causes. Al-Tabataba'i says people delay what they regard lightly, and, citing 8:24, that the warning especially fits reform of the heart beyond outward bodily acts. Islahi urges belief before seizure, and says the Qur'an's qualities warrant wholehearted acceptance lest denial bring unimaginable punishment."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q01", "question": "How does 'an taqula' depend on the preceding commands?", "turns_on": "Whether the prevention sense is expressed by purpose syntax, an omitted noun, or an omitted negative.", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q01/p1", "position": "It is a purpose clause: return, submit, and follow revelation lest a soul say this.", "reasons": "Al-Farra, Tabari, Baghawi and others compare 16:15; Tha'labi also cites 2:184. Ibn Atiyya attaches it to anibu, Ibn Ashur to 39:54-55 with an omitted purpose lam. Al-Mubarrad and Zajjaj paraphrase it as acting before remorse or fearing the utterance."}, {"id": "39:56/q01/p2", "position": "An omitted noun of aversion, caution, or fear supplies the negative purpose.", "reasons": "Nahhas gives karahata an taqula; Kufans say li-alla, Basrans posit karaha or hidhār. Zamakhshari supplies aversion; Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa supply 'we warned you for fear.' Al-Alusi prefers aversion over fear and says it denotes lack of approval, not God's will. Islahi posits an omitted governing noun."}, {"id": "39:56/q01/p3", "position": "A negative la is omitted after an.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur prefers this account to al-Kashshaf's fear paraphrase, citing 6:155-157 and 4:135 as parallels."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q02", "question": "Which soul does the indefinite 'nafs' designate?", "turns_on": "Whether the indefinite is partitive, generic, or singles out an exceptional sinner.", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q02/p1", "position": "Some souls, particularly unbelieving or polytheist souls.", "reasons": "Nasafi and Zamakhshari say the partitive indefinite can mean some unbelievers. Abu Hayyan prefers this; Al-Alusi says warning any possible member is enough. Ibn Ashur calls it a category of polytheist souls and cites 81:14 and Labid."}, {"id": "39:56/q02/p2", "position": "Many or every soul subject to this warning.", "reasons": "Razi relates generic regret after neglected obedience; Qurtubi, Baydawi, Samin and Al-Alusi cite al-A'sha's indefinite noun for a group. Bursevi says the warning may cover all; Biqai says anyone might be intended."}, {"id": "39:56/q02/p3", "position": "One unusually persistent sinner or one facing exceptional punishment.", "reasons": "Razi, Zamakhshari, Nasafi and Samin report this possibility; Al-Alusi finds it unpersuasive."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q03", "question": "What does the word 'nafs' itself mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q03/p1", "position": "A person or self.", "reasons": "Jishumi equates nafs with dhat and connects it with preciousness, the self being an animal's most precious part. Asad says nafs normally means a human being and renders its pronouns masculine despite Arabic feminine gender."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q04", "question": "Is the soul's saying an audible cry or inward speech?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q04/p1", "position": "It may be an audible lament or inward speech.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the audible cry adds to hidden regret, while the wording also permits inner speech."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q05", "question": "What is the meaning of 'hasrata'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q05/p1", "position": "Intense sorrow or regret over irrecoverable neglect and loss.", "reasons": "Suddi glosses it as regret; Tha'labi, Baghawi, Ibn Jawzi, Tabarsi, Bursevi, Ibn Ashur and al-Majma' stress loss beyond recovery. Jishumi links its root to a camel exhausted at journey's end; Bursevi cites sorrow leaving the soul exhausted, and says ignorance is stripped away. Al-Farra calls it the most intense remorse."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q06", "question": "Why address regret with 'ya'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q06/p1", "position": "The speaker summons personified regret because its moment has arrived, making the warning and lament forceful.", "reasons": "Zajjaj says regret has seized the speaker; Azharī, Sibawayh, Baghawi, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur say 'come, now is your time.' Jishumi says regret cannot literally be summoned, so the cry alerts listeners. Basrans compare 'O wonder'; Ibn Jinni says this would be the time to call regret if it could be called. Nahhas says vocative is stronger than a report."}, {"id": "39:56/q06/p2", "position": "It expresses a plea for aid or an exclamation of utmost grief.", "reasons": "Farra says Arabic changes the possessive ending in appeals into a plea form; Bursevi calls it an appeal for help. Al-Farra elsewhere glosses it 'what regret!'."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q07", "question": "How is 'ya hasrata' read and analyzed?", "turns_on": "Whether the ending is possessive ya, its alif substitute, both together, a dual, or a pausal ha; connected ha is disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q07/p1", "position": "The common form ends in alif replacing the speaker's possessive ya.", "reasons": "Tabari compares ya waylata and ya nadama; Farra, Tha'labi, Mawardi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Jawzi, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Samin, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur explain the alif as easier and allowing a prolonged cry. Abu Hayyan reports the majority reading."}, {"id": "39:56/q07/p2", "position": "The original possessive ya is retained: ya hasrati.", "reasons": "Zajjaj permits it; Ibn Atiyya calls it the form of most readers in his account. Ibn Jawzi names Hasan, Abu al-Aliya, Abu Imran and Abu al-Jawza; Samin and Al-Alusi report Abu Ja'far. Baydawi and Nasafi note the variant."}, {"id": "39:56/q07/p3", "position": "Abu Ja'far also reads ya hasratay, retaining both alif and added possessive ya.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports open and silent ya and Ibn Jammaz's kasra-ta/silent-ya variant; Ibn Jinni objects to combining substitute and original, but Tabarsi cites Farazdaq and Abu Zayd as parallels. Nashr says Ibn Jammaz has open ya, Ibn Wardan both open and silent, and al-Jazari defends the silent transmission. Samin offers dialectal defense and weaker alternative analyses; Biqai says it intensifies grief."}, {"id": "39:56/q07/p4", "position": "Ya hasratay may be a dual, expressing repeated or two regrets.", "reasons": "Abu al-Fadl al-Razi gives loss of Paradise and entry into Fire as the two; Samin notes expected contracted morphology as an objection, and cites the dialect retaining dual alif. Sahib al-Kashf prefers an emphatic dual like labbayk; Al-Alusi prefers intensity because Judgement Day has many sorrows."}, {"id": "39:56/q07/p5", "position": "A final ha may be appended in lament or at a pause.", "reasons": "Farra adduces Abu Fuq'as/Banu Asad's y

{"id": "39:56/q08", "question": "What does 'ala' add to the lament?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q08/p1", "position": "It depicts regret as pressing firmly upon what was lost.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says 'upon' is the usual link with hasra and makes the regret cling to its object; Al-Alusi treats it as causal."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q09", "question": "How does 'ma' function in 'ala ma farrattu'?", "turns_on": "Whether ma makes an action noun or refers to neglected things.", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q09/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun marker: 'for my neglect.'", "reasons": "Nasafi compares 9:25; Abu Hayyan, Samin, Bursevi, Al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur agree. Al-Alusi compares 2:185."}, {"id": "39:56/q09/p2", "position": "It can be a relative pronoun: 'what I neglected.'", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur supplies a deleted object pronoun after farraṭt and makes 'in God's side' describe that object."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q10", "question": "What does 'farrattu' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q10/p1", "position": "I neglected or fell short of what was due before its opportunity passed.", "reasons": "Muqatil says neglect; Ibn Atiyya says falling short of what was required. Tabarsi and al-Majma' define omission before time passes; Raghib contrasts tafrit with excess in pressing ahead. Biqai stresses broken trust and lost order; KuranYolu prefers Ibn Ashur's required-duty sense."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q11", "question": "What does 'fi janb Allah' mean?", "turns_on": "Which figurative relation 'side' denotes—command, duty, remembrance, reward, path, nearness, essence, or application to the Imams—and whether a bodily sense is possible.", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q11/p1", "position": "God's command or affair, including the commanded path of faith.", "reasons": "Mujahid and Suddi say command; Ibn Arafa and others use affair. Zajjaj specifies monotheism and the Messenger's prophethood. Tabari says failure to act on commands in worldly life; Ibn Atiyya includes law and faith. Arabic idiom and Kathir's poetry attest janb as an affair."}, {"id": "39:56/q11/p2", "position": "God's obedience, duty or right is what was neglected.", "reasons": "Hasan repeatedly says obedience; Sa'id ibn Jubayr says God's due. Baydawi cites Sabiq al-Barbari's verse for the right owed a beloved; Samin derives right from side. Burhan says neglect cannot apply to a bodily flank. Tabatabai specifies worshipping God alone without disobedience. KuranYolu prefers obedience."}, {"id": "39:56/q11/p3", "position": "Remembrance of God, especially the Quran and acting on it.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Dahhak, Ikrima and some Mujahid reports say remembrance; Nahhas and Qurtubi specify the Quran and practice. Abdullah's variant reads fi dhikr Allah."}, {"id": "39:56/q11/p4", "position": "God's reward, particularly Paradise, was forfeited.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and Abu Ubayda give reward; Naqqash specifies Paradise. The nearness interpretation also points to Paradise."}, {"id": "39:56/q11/p5", "position": "The path or side leading to God's pleasure and reward.", "reasons": "Arabic uses janb for a side, means or road. Tha'labi quotes the poet contrasting ruler and people and one enduring bitterness for another's sake; Zajjaj connects the path with faith. Ibn Ashur's master-and-preserve picture lets the side remain concrete within a tableau."}, {"id": "39:56/q11/p6", "position": "Seeking nearness to God, ultimately Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Farra explains janb by neighborliness and 4:36's companion at one's side; Mawardi speaks of seeking proximity. Study Quran includes bodily, emotional and spiritual closeness. Al-Alusi rejects this reading as needing an extra metaphor and reducing to obedience."}, {"id": "39:56/q11/p7", "position": "God's essence is meant, with an omitted related noun in some accounts.", "reasons": "Mawardi reports Hasan; Baghawi records the view, Baydawi adds omitted annexation, Nasafi lists it. Al-Alusi rejects it as awkward even figuratively."}, {"id": "39:56/q11/p8", "position": "The Imams are God's side as an application of the verse.", "reasons": "Tabrisi transmits Abu Ja'far via al-Ayyashi and Abu al-Jarud. Tabatabai says reports apply the verses to the Imams' Shi'a and calls them application rather than primary exegesis."}, {"id": "39:56/q11/p9", "position": "The phrase is a figure for what belongs to God, not a divine bodily limb.", "reasons": "Razi rejects physical parts; Abu Hayyan says bodily attribution is impossible. Raghib traces bodily side to neighboring direction; Razi and al-Imam extend part/side to a necessary attendant, while Al-Alusi rejects al-Imam's explicit-metaphor analysis. Baydawi and Abu Hayyan compare putting virtues in a man's dome; Ibn Ashur pictures a master's neglected preserve."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q12", "question": "Is there a variant reading for 'fi janb Allah'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q12/p1", "position": "A reading attributed to Abdullah has 'fi dhikr Allah' ('in God's remembrance').", "reasons": "Nasafi and Al-Alusi report this wording; it supports the remembrance interpretation."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q13", "question": "Why say 'Allah' rather than use a pronoun?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q13/p1", "position": "Naming God heightens the warning about the Supreme King's right.", "reasons": "Biqai says this right was neither forgotten nor treated lightly."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q14", "question": "How is 'wa-in kuntu lamina' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is a circumstantial modifier or a separate report; the particle and plural also need parsing.", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q14/p1", "position": "In is lightened emphatic inna; the lam distinguishes it from negative in.", "reasons": "Bursevi, Al-Alusi and Tabatabai give this parsing; Ibn Ashur calls the lam differentiating."}, {"id": "39:56/q14/p2", "position": "The clause is circumstantial: the person neglected duty while mocking.", "reasons": "Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Zamakhshari, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur say the simultaneous mockery aggravates neglect."}, {"id": "39:56/q14/p3", "position": "It is an independent account of the speaker's former state.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Bahr reject the circumstantial parse; it reports worldly mockery and intensifies regret."}, {"id": "39:56/q14/p4", "position": "The masculine plural means 'among the people or group of mockers' although nafs is feminine.", "reasons": "Nahhas answers the grammatical objection by supplying group, people or folk."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q15", "question": "Whom or what did the speaker mock?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q15/p1", "position": "God's religion, scripture, Messenger, command, and believers.", "reasons": "Tabari lists command, scripture, Messenger and believers; Suddi specifies Prophet, Book and message. Biqai calls the mockery habitual arrogance; Ibn Kathir contrasts scoffing with conviction."}, {"id": "39:56/q15/p2", "position": "The phrase describes a life of mockery, play, falsehood, or worship of others.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports the broader explanation; Ibn Kathir says the former conduct was scoffing rather than certain faith."}, {"id": "39:56/q15/p3", "position": "Sakhir means one who mocks; one gloss takes the mockers as foolish or senile.", "reasons": "Damghani groups 2:212 and 49:11 under mockery; Ibn Atiyya and Tabatabai derive the active participle from sakhira. Itqan supplies the foolish/senile gloss."}]}

{"id": "39:56/q17", "question": "What does the verse warn people to do before remorse comes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q17/p1", "position": "Repent, submit and follow revelation now; regret after the chance passes is futile.", "reasons": "Rummani, Baqillani and Burhan call the cry the strongest warning against neglect. {"id": "39:56/q25", "question": "How does Aisha's exoneration narrative enter the material?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q25/p1", "position": "Reports recount the slander, her distress, revelation of innocence, and consequences for the accusers.", "reasons": "Ibn Hisham says Aisha hoped for a dream rather than revelation, then the Prophet publicly recited her vindication and ordered penalties for Mistah, Hassan and Hamna. {"id": "39:56/q27", "question": "What Qur'anic notation and pronunciation conventions are noted here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q27/p1", "position": "Vowel, assimilation and concealment signs follow established notation; the ta after ta in farraṭtu is marked with sukun.", "reasons": "Itqan contrasts early colored dot vowels with al-Khalil's modern letter-derived signs, doubled tanwin, red omitted alif and hamza, red mim for iqlab, and assimilation marking. It singles out ṭāʾ before tāʾ in farraṭtu."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q28", "question": "How do cited discussions frame interpretation of divine expressions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q28/p1", "position": "Interpret the apparent Arabic sense as God's right or obedience while affirming divine transcendence.", "reasons": "Itqan cites Ibn al-Salah on early practice, Ibn Burhan's preference for interpretation, Ibn Daqiq al-Id's allowance of interpretations close to Arabic and suspension on remote ones, then applies the apparent sense here to God's due."}, {"id": "39:56/q28/p2", "position": "An estimated aversion in the purpose clause does not settle the doctrine of divine will.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says aversion here is the opposite of approval and does not entail the Mu'tazilite position."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q29", "question": "What general Qur'anic study methodology is recorded in these notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q29/p1", "position": "Al-Itqan arranges Qur'anic studies into eighty kinds, potentially more than three hundred if separated.", "reasons": "Itqan compares earlier works by Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Sakhawi, Abu Shama and Shidhila, judging them smaller samples."}]}
{"id": "39:56/q30", "question": "Why use declarative wording for a directive?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:56/q30/p1", "position": "A declarative prohibition can be stronger because a prophetic report is treated as unable to fail.", "reasons": "Burhan quotes Nawawi's examples of 'he does not propose' and 'bid,' and notes that 'do not ask' may be read as statement or direct prohibition."}]}
{"id": "39:57/q01", "question": "How does this saying join the other sayings, and who says them?", "turns_on": "Whether the alternatives distribute speeches among groups or follow one condemned person's sequence of thoughts; Bursawī gives both possibilities.", "positions": [{"id": "39:57/q01/p1", "position": "The sayings are alternatives voiced by different groups of condemned people.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the later aw taqūlu clauses coordinate with the first an taqūla. Qatāda, as reported by al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Durr, assigns neglect, the guidance plea and the return wish to first, second and third groups respectively. Elmalılı calls this speaker another soul. Bursawī offers different groups as an alternative."}, {"id": "39:57/q01/p2", "position": "The three sayings trace the condemned person's unfolding thought: regret, excuse about guidance, then wish to return.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī connects the warnings and commands to these three regrets. {"id": "39:57/q03", "question": "How does the construction لو أن work here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:57/q03/p1", "position": "After لو, a nominal clause normally enters through أن rather than beginning with a bare noun.", "reasons": "Sībawayh contrasts لو with لولا, which can be followed by nouns, and cites 17:100. His wider discussion shows that an أن-clause can depend on what precedes: أحقا and أكبر ظنك support a raised construction, with a possible reversed analysis; Yūnus transmits the Arabs' recitation of al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur, and al-Khalīl compares its threat with الرحيل بعد غد. Al-ʿAbdī, ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa and al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī supply further poetic attestations. In لا محالة أنك, he supplies an omitted من. أما licenses إن through its meaning مهما يكن من شيء; his examples distinguish report from location, allow أن after جهد رأيي, and permit a preceding temporal phrase such as اليوم or بعد. شد ما and عز ما أنك mean حقا أنك and may be analyzed like نعم ما. In كما أنه the kāf governs أن while extra ما distinguishes it from كأن; poetry can omit ما. His separate singular فريق and قعيد analogy illustrates number usage in the same grammatical discussion."}]}
